rows: Most jumping spiders build their colour from two pigments in the large front eyes. One peaks in the ultraviolet near 360 nm and the other in the green near 530 nm. Red and orange have no receptor of their own, so the picture shifts them toward dark green.

The sharp front eyes carry the colour. The side eyes give a grey, single-pigment picture at lower sharpness, so the colour is kept to the sharp patch. Later work on the genes suggests the side eyes may carry some colour, which this picture leaves out.

Each front eye has a narrow strip of retina, about 5 degrees across and 20 high. A typical jumping spider can pick out about 3.8 cycles per degree there, around an eighth of your sharpness. Portia is the star, at 12.5 cycles per degree.
The six side eyes together cover close to the whole circle around the animal. They are blurry, with about 0.3 to 1.3 cycles per degree in the front side eyes, so most of the picture is soft.

With the front eyes covered, the side eyes behave as if completely blind to stationary things. A light that only switches on and off draws no reaction. Outside the sharp patch, still things fade away.

The front retinas sweep side to side across what they inspect, at least 2 degrees wide, once every 1 to 2 seconds. They also twist about 25 degrees each way, taking about 2 seconds and pausing for 2 to 5 seconds at each end. After the front eyes inspect a place, the side eyes ignore it for about 5 seconds.

The app draws the side eyes in grey and the sharp patch in colour. It uses the phone's blue channel in place of ultraviolet and starts the sharp patch at the centre of the picture. The size of the ignored place after an inspection is a guess. The squeeze into the frame, the stamped images and the painted blur are the app's drawings.
A third colour in some species
The Habronattus spiders have a filtered third receptor that reaches into the red, near 626 nm. This picture leaves it out because most jumping spiders have two pigments.

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree and a squid about 6.6, against a person's 30. Some small octopus species fall between 3 and 7, a cuttlefish is put near 8, and a newly hatched oval squid manages only 0.63. The picture is blurred to a middling value for adults.

Almost all of these animals have a single visual pigment, with its peak between 470 and 500 nanometres, near 480 in octopus. With one pigment they cannot tell hues apart, and tests on octopus and on cuttlefish agree. The picture keeps one shade and only the brightness changes.

Young oval squid see about 311 to 329 degrees around themselves. One eye of a cuttlefish covers 253 degrees, and the two eyes of a cuttlefish overlap by 86 degrees in front. Octopuses have no significant overlap. The camera holds a slice of this wide field.

The receptors of an octopus are packed most densely in a horizontal stripe across the middle of the retina, about 55,000 per square millimetre against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edge. Cuttlefish and squid also have a streak or a patch of crowding. A sharp band runs across the picture.

An octopus pupil is round in the dark and shrinks to a horizontal slit in bright light, down to about a tenth of its dark area. A cuttlefish can shrink its pupil to 3 percent of the widest opening. The picture uses the slit.

A squid stops seeing flicker near 51 a second and a cuttlefish near 30. An octopus reaches 72 in bright light and only 20 when the light is far dimmer. A person stops near 60, so only the octopus in bright light slows the picture a little.

Octopuses can pick out differences in the direction of polarised light that a person cannot see at all. Their eyes have two sensitive planes, one horizontal and one vertical. The typical octopus threshold is very fine, at 0.01 on the scale used by the study.

The squid value of 6.56 for the whole picture, the width of the squeezed field, the height of the sharp band, the sharpness given to that band, the single-shade mapping, the slowing of the octopus picture and the polarised overlay are the app's own settings, placed inside what the records describe.

Four pairs of eyes see the rest of the world. The side eyes see movement across nearly the whole circle around the spider, and they are much blurrier.

Jumping spiders have two colour receptors in the principal eyes, one ultraviolet and one green. Saitis barbipes and Plexippus validus both showed these two classes, so the picture is a dichromat's picture.
The side eyes respond to movement and little else, and a still object stays unseen until it moves. Metaphidippus harfordi turned only to targets that moved.

rows: A honeybee can only just tell apart stripes about four degrees wide. Its picture is roughly a hundred times coarser than a person's, so fine detail melts into a soft blur.
The two compound eyes together see about 300 degrees around the body. Only a small patch below and behind is blind, and the eyes overlap in front and above.
A bee has receptors that peak in the ultraviolet near 346 nm, the blue near 430 nm and the green near 540 nm. It sees ultraviolet light, which people cannot see.
A honeybee can follow a flicker of about 200 times a second in bright light. In dimmer light of 300 lux the limit falls to about 144 times a second.
About a third of 80 flower species in one study carry patterns in ultraviolet. A person sees some of these flowers as a plain colour, while a bee sees a dark centre or guide marks.
A ring of ultraviolet receptors along the top rim of the bee's eye reads the pattern of polarised light in the sky. The bee uses it as a compass when the sun is hidden.

The colour shift is the app's choice. It follows a common convention in which ultraviolet shows as blue, blue as green and green as red, and red is dropped. The speed-up that hints at fast flicker and the polarisation hint are also the app's own drawings.

rows: In every whale and seal studied, the retina has only one kind of cone, tuned to long wavelengths, and no blue-sensitive cone. In dolphins and porpoises that cone peaks near 523 nanometres. We draw the picture with a single colour sensor, so colours collapse into lighter and darker shades.

Baleen whales and sperm whales have lost the genes for their cone pigments and rely on rods alone. A manatee has two kinds of cone, and a California sea lion picked out colours in behaviour tests. The single sensor picture is a middle case for the group.

A humpback whale resolves about 3.95 cycles per degree and a Bryde's whale 4.8. A false killer whale, a Pacific white-sided dolphin and a beluga managed 2.6 to 3.3. A harbour seal reaches 11.5 under water, and a manatee only 1.6. Most of these values are estimated from the retina. A person resolves about 30, so we blur the picture to 3.95.
A dolphin's eyes sit on the sides of its head and give a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees. The two eyes overlap by only 20 to 30 degrees. We squeeze the picture to about 125 degrees.

A bottlenose dolphin sees low light half a log unit better than a person, about three times better, but 0.2 log units worse in bright light. Dolphins, harbour seals and elephant seals have a reflective layer behind the retina. Manatees lack it. We brighten the picture about three times.

Seal whiskers are most sensitive to vibration between 10 and 100 hertz, and a harbour seal can follow a fish's wake for up to 30 seconds after the fish has passed. A phone has no way to give this, so it is left out.

The blur, the squeeze of the field, the brightening, the single colour sensor and the strength of the reflective sheen are the app's choices, set from the records above. A humpback whale's sharpness stands for the whole group, though seals see sharper and manatees see softer. No record gives the strength of the sheen, so we set it by eye.

A bottlenose dolphin sends clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz, far above what a phone microphone can hear. With the microphone on, the app can draw rings from the sounds it does hear. The drawing is the app's.

rows: A scorpion's eyes can apparently take in the whole way around its body. The two middle eyes together cover a full circle, with about forty degrees of overlap above the animal.

The pair of eyes in the middle of the head are the main eyes. They give a fairly sharp picture and tell shapes apart. The side eyes, three to five pairs, seem to notice mostly changes in how bright the light is.
Buthid scorpions have five pairs of small side eyes. The first three are about 0.3 mm across and the last two are about 0.12 mm across in one species.
Electrical recordings from the eyes of two scorpion genera peak in blue light at 470 nm and in green light at 525 nm. The side eyes also respond in the ultraviolet.
Scorpions are active at night and their eyes can sense starlight. In one species the middle eyes are about a thousand times more sensitive at night than by day.

No record gives how much detail a scorpion sees, so this view shows a coarse picture. The extra brightness, the recolouring from two colour peaks, and the way the all-round view is pressed into the phone are the app's own.

A scorpion feels the ground through its legs and can locate prey up to about 50 cm away by the waves it makes in sand. It tastes the air and ground with its comb-like pectines and feels wind with fine hairs. The camera records none of this.

claims.how: Both records state a 360 degree field of view for scorpions.
The matrix is built from the two peaks, 470 nm (R5) and 525 nm (R9), that the records give; the mapping to screen colours is the app's.
Pigment peaks 470 and 525 nm are taken directly from the two records and turned into a colour matrix by the app.

rows: A humpback whale resolves about 3.3 cycles per degree and a Bryde's whale about 4.8, both in water. Harbour seals reach about 11.5 underwater, so this view is a rough middle of those figures.
Dolphins see a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, with their two eyes overlapping only a little. Their eyes sit to the side of the head.

Most whales have only rod cells in the dim light, so they see almost no colour. Where a green-sensitive pigment is recorded, a harbour porpoise or pilot whale reads about 520 nanometres, and the picture shows that green range.
Cetaceans have a reflective layer behind the retina. Seals have one too, and the picture lifts the shadows a little in the dark.
The gain, the fade of still things, the colour strength and the sharp middle are the app's own choices, not records.

spectrum.note: colour drawn from the three cone peaks of a macaque

rows: A cynomolgus monkey has three kinds of cone, most sensitive near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres. Macaques and people share this three-cone plan, so colours look much as they do to you.

Owl monkeys and bushbabies have a single kind of M/L cone and lack colour vision. Male marmosets have two kinds of cone. Howler monkeys have three. This view shows the three-cone picture of a macaque.

Young rhesus monkeys reached 26.3 cycles per degree on a grating test, close to a person's 30. A marmoset's cone mosaic could carry about 30. A grey mouse lemur resolves only about 4.9, so smaller primates see less fine detail.
A model of a chimpanzee-like skull gives a sideways reach of 115 degrees for the eye, against 136.1 degrees for a person. Scaling your 180 degrees by that ratio gives about 152 degrees.
The owl monkey is the only night-active monkey. Its retina is fully adapted to the dark and its fovea is only rudimentary.

The macaque's cone peaks are used for the whole group, and the app chose how they map onto your colours. We draw no dim-light change and no special fovea, because the records give no numbers for them.
